query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys, the nature of the X element (Al, Si, or Mn) controls the protective oxide behavior at temperatures above 900 °C by governing both the diffusion kinetics and the phase stability of the oxide scale. Alloys containing Al (and possibly Si) preferentially form a slow-growing, dense, and coherent oxide (primarily Al2O3 or a silica-based oxide) with a low lattice mismatch to the substrate, while Mn-bearing alloys develop rapidly growing, porous manganese oxides that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state where X is varied among Al, Si, and Mn.
generation.intervention: Expose alloy samples with controlled variations in the X element to oxidative (and/or corrosive) atmospheres at temperatures exceeding 900 °C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (above 900 °C) exposure in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere for sufficient durations to allow oxide-scale development and evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: The diffusion behavior and oxidation kinetics of the X element, which determine the microstructure and adhesion of the resulting oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: In alloys enriched with Al (or Si), the slower diffusion kinetics lead to the preferential formation of a dense, coherent oxide (Al2O3/silica-based) with minimal lattice mismatch and low growth stress. In contrast, in Mn-containing alloys, the higher diffusivity promotes rapid oxidation forming less coherent, porous manganese oxide phases that develop high internal stresses and crack or spall.
generation.predicted_outcome: Al-containing (or Si-enriched) HEAs will exhibit continuous, adherent, slow-growing protective oxide scales that persist during prolonged high-temperature exposure, while Mn-containing alloys are predicted to form unstable, rapidly thickening oxide layers that spall or crack, thereby degrading the oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: A comparison against alloys in which X is Mn (or where the protective element is absent), which typically develop non-protective, easily spalling oxide layers.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX HEAs in both single- and multiphase solid-solution states under high-temperature (above 900 °C) conditions in oxidative or corrosive environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative differences in diffusion rates and lattice mismatches across different compositions, especially in multiphase alloys, need further investigation. The effect of minor compositional variations on the oxide growth kinetics also introduces uncertainty in predicting exact rates of oxidation and oxide scale coherence.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with controlled X element variations (Al, Si, and Mn). Expose these samples to an oxidative atmosphere at, for example, 950 °C for a fixed duration (e.g., 24 hours). Use in situ high-temperature XRD, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to characterize the oxide scale phases, morphology, microstructural integrity, and diffusion profiles across the oxide-metal interface.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification of oxide scales via XRD
Morphological assessment and scale continuity/surface cracking using SEM
Elemental diffusion profiles and scale composition using EDS mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments show that alloys with Al (or Si) do not develop a coherent, adherent, and slow-growing protective oxide scale—or if Mn-containing alloys produce oxide scales that are as coherent and protective as those formed by Al/Si alloys—then the hypothesis that the specific element controlling diffusion and oxide phase stability governs oxide layer performance would be falsified.

## Abstract
This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. ## Abstract
AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition

## Abstract
AbstractThe oxidation behavior of an equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co high-entropy alloy (HEA) processed by 3D laser printing was investigated at 700 °C and 900 °C. The oxidation kinetics of the alloy followed the parabolic rate law, and the oxidation rate constant increased with the rising of the temperature. Inward diffusion of oxygen and outward diffusion of cations took place during the high-temperature oxidation process. A spinel-type oxide was formed on the surface, and the thickness of the oxide layer increased with the rising of experimental temperature or time. The exfoliation of the oxide layer took place when the test was operated at 900 °C over 12 h. During oxidation tests, the matrix was propped open by oxides and was segmented into small pieces. The formation of loose structures had great effects on the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the HEA.Keywords: metals and alloys, 3D printing, oxidation
